claims.claim: The rates of scrambling are higher for the TMEM16F F518H mutant than the open WT TMEM16F, but there were no noticeable differences in how lipids enter the pathway or how long they take to transition.
claims.source: Although the rates of scrambling are higher for the mutant than the open WT TMEM16F, there were no noticeable differences in how lipids enter the pathway or how long they take to transition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Both the Ca2+-bound (PDB ID 5OYB) and the Ca2+-free (PDB ID 5OYG) experimental structures of TMEM16A failed to induce scrambling in the CGMD simulations.
claims.source: Finally, we simulated six structures of mouse TMEM16A, which functions as an ion channel but lacks lipid scrambling activity (Paulino et al., 2017). As expected, both the Ca2+-bound (PDB ID 5OYB) and the Ca2+-free (PDB ID 5OYG) experimental structures failed to induce scrambling in the CGMD simulations, as did one alternative and two ion conduction-competent structures that were obtained from AAMD (see Appendix 1—Methods for details).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and comparison with experimental findings.

claims.claim: A TMEM16A state with an open hydrophilic groove predicted by Jia and Chen (5OYB*) scrambled a single lipid through each groove in a manner nearly identical to the scramblases.
claims.source: However, a TMEM16A state with an open hydrophilic groove predicted by Jia and Chen (5OYB*, simulations initiated from PDB ID 5OYB; Jia and Chen, 2021) did scramble a single lipid through each groove in a manner nearly identical to the scramblases (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A, E and Figure 3—video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: 92% of the observed scrambling events occur along TM4 and TM6 with headgroups embedded in the open hydrated groove, in line with the credit card model.
claims.source: In our CGMD simulations, 92% of the observed scrambling events occur along TM4 and TM6 with headgroups embedded in the open hydrated groove, in line with the credit card model, which we refer to as 'in-the-groove' scrambling (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is presented in a table.

claims.claim: All TMEM16 structures thin the membrane to 23 Å or less, which is at least 7 Å thinner than the bulk membrane thickness (30 Å), regardless of scrambling activity.
claims.source: Interestingly, all the TMEM16 structures included in this study thin the membrane to 23 Å or less, which is at least 7 Å thinner than the bulk membrane thickness (30 Å), regardless of scrambling activity (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: Negligible scrambling activity (0–1 events in the groove) was observed in grooves that fail to thin the membrane to less than 14 Å and do not or very rarely sample TM4-TM6 distances above 6 Å.
claims.source: We observed negligible scrambling activity (0–1 events in the groove) in grooves that fail to thin the membrane to less than 14 Å and at the same time do not or very rarely sample TM4-TM6 distances above 6 Å (Figure 3A, upper left quadrant).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: All active scramblers have a minimal bilayer thickness below 14 Å.
claims.source: On the other hand, all active scramblers have a minimal bilayer thickness below 14 Å.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: The highest scrambling rates were observed in grooves that remain open, with TM4–TM6 distances above 6 Å, throughout most of the simulation.
claims.source: Among these structures, we observed the highest scrambling rates in grooves that remain open, with TM4–TM6 distances above 6 Å, throughout most of the simulation (shaded region).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: Two TMEM16F structures (PDB ID 8B8J and 6QP6*) spent less than half of their simulation time in an open configuration and had scrambling rates similar to or less than half of rates for the open scramblases.
claims.source: To the left of this shaded area, there are two TMEM16F structures (PDB ID 8B8J and 6QP6*) that spent less than half of their simulation time in an open configuration (note large error bars and Figure 3B) and had scrambling rates similar to (PDB ID 8B8J) or less than half of (6QP6*) rates for the open scramblases (PDB IDs 6QM6, 7RXG, and 5OC9).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves.
claims.source: Although these results indicate that scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves, we want to clarify that lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness.
claims.source: Although these results indicate that scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves, we want to clarify that lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of the dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed <14 Å membrane thickness (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The extremely thin membranes are likely correlated with groove opening, rather than being an independent contributing factor to lipid scrambling.
claims.source: Therefore, we argue that the extremely thin membranes are likely correlated with groove opening, rather than being an independent contributing factor to lipid scrambling.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the simulation data and represents the authors' argument.

claims.claim: The major determinant of lipid scrambling by TMEM16s is dilation of the TM4/TM6 groove.
claims.source: Thus, the major determinant of lipid scrambling by TMEM16s is dilation of the TM4/TM6 groove.
claims.evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: Hydrophobic residues (H/F518, W619, and M522) at the midpoint of the TMEM16F pathway dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through.
claims.source: Upon closer inspection of TMEM16F, we noticed that hydrophobic residues (H/F518, W619, and M522) at the midpoint of the pathway, previously identified as an activation gate (Le et al., 2019b), dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C; Figure 3—videos 3 and 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures and videos.

claims.claim: The distribution of the groove distances is similar for both TMEM16F structures that exhibit scrambling (8B8J and 6QP6*), but the WT open structure (6QP6*) has half the single subunit scrambling rate.
claims.source: Although the distribution of the groove distances is similar for both TMEM16F structures that exhibit scrambling (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B), the WT open structure (6QP6*) has half the single subunit scrambling rate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Similar fluctuations were observed in both subunits of the open asymmetric TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) which transiently constrict the lipid pathway at Y366/I370/T435/L436.
claims.source: We observed similar fluctuations in both subunits of the open asymmetric TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) which transiently constrict the lipid pathway at Y366/I370/T435/L436 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 6A, D; Figure 3—videos 2 and 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures and videos.

claims.claim: The TMEM16K subunit with more scrambling activity (eight times more) spent more time in an open-groove configuration.
claims.source: Again, we observed that the subunit with more scrambling activity (eight times more) spent more time in an open-groove configuration (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open for TMEM16K and F.
claims.source: Qualitatively, scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open for TMEM16K and F (black dots in Figure 3B), while the consistently open Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 structure (PDB ID 4WIS) allows lipid headgroups to scramble in an uninterrupted fashion (Figure 3B, Figure 3—video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qualitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure and video.

claims.claim: The predicted ion-conductive state of TMEM16A (5OYB*) samples an average TM4–TM6 distance very close, but just below, the empirically determined 6 Å threshold for scrambling.
claims.source: Although all structures of TMEM16A, which is not a scramblase, have negligible scrambling in the groove, we did observe two events for a predicted ion-conductive state (5OYB*) which samples an average TM4–TM6 distance very close, but just below, to the empirically determined 6 Å threshold for scrambling (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Lipid headgroups are observed throughout the TMEM16A pathway, but the flow of lipid is obstructed by residues at the center of the groove (I550, I551, and K645), and they more rarely separate to allow lipids to pass.
claims.source: We observed lipid headgroups throughout the pathway, but just as for the TMEM16F and K structures, the flow of lipid is obstructed by residues at the center of the groove (I550, I551, and K645), and in TMEM16A they more rarely separate to allow lipids to pass (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Lipids in the TMEM16A pore are notably more stagnant than in the open TMEM16Fs and appear to be stabilized by electrostatic interactions with two charged residues, E633 and K645.
claims.source: Lipids are also notably more stagnant in the pore than in the open TMEM16Fs and appear to be stabilized by electrostatic interactions with two charged residues, E633 and K645 (Figure 3—video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a video.

claims.claim: Scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the TMEM16 family.
claims.source: Despite these individual differences in groove dynamics, scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the family.
claims.evidence: This claim is a generalization based on analysis of simulation data across multiple family members.

claims.claim: Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly, with dwell times for individual lipids below 20 ns.
claims.source: Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly, with dwell times for individual lipids below 20 ns.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: Longer dwell times were observed for TMEM16K and TMEM16F at the groove constriction points, whereas in other scramblases, the dwell times are more evenly distributed along the groove.
claims.source: However, we observed longer dwell times for TMEM16K and TMEM16F at the groove constriction points, whereas in other scramblases, the dwell times are more evenly distributed along the groove (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: Among the scramblases, the free energy profile for lipids moving through the open groove is barrierless (<1 kT).
claims.source: Among the scramblases, the free energy profile for lipids moving through the open groove is barrierless (<1 kT) (Appendix 1—figure 3A) with similar kinetics among the homologs and a mean diffusion coefficient between 10 and 16 Å2/ns (Appendix 1—figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by free energy calculations from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Scrambling events enter and leave the groove at random locations with only 3–10% of events passing through the high-density lipid regions on lower TM4 and upper TM6/TM8.
claims.source: Scrambling events also enter and leave the groove at random locations (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5) with only 3–10% of events passing through the high-density lipid regions on lower TM4 and upper TM6/TM8 (Figure 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: Four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove were previously hypothesized to help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids.
claims.source: We previously identified four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove that we hypothesized help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids (Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim references a previous hypothesis from a cited study and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: CGMD of nhTMEM16 shows that although the four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble.
claims.source: However, our CGMD of the same nhTMEM16 structure shows that although these residues have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases.
claims.source: Lastly, the in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases (Appendix 1—figure 5), indicating lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
claims.source: Lastly, the in-the-groove scrambling events were Poisson distributed for all open and transiently open scramblases (Appendix 1—figure 5), indicating lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the Poisson distribution of scrambling events.

claims.claim: Permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average.
claims.source: As expected, permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average, while dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 permeation events per μs on average.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of water permeation from simulation data.

claims.claim: Dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 water permeation events per μs on average.
claims.source: As expected, permeation through the closed scramblase structures was low, <30 events per μs on average, while dilated TM4/TM6 grooves (five out of six Ca2+-bound) support 300–550 permeation events per μs on average.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of water permeation from simulation data.

claims.claim: Even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed and intermediate states, including the TMEM16A ion channel path, it remains hydrated with the waters shielded from the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
claims.source: Nonetheless, even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed and intermediate states, including the TMEM16A ion channel path, it remains hydrated with the waters shielded from the hydrophobic core of the membrane (Appendix 1—figure 2A, closed).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: In open grooves, the water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets.
claims.source: We qualitatively observed that in open grooves, the water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets (Appendix 1—figure 2A, open) as seen in fully atomistic simulations (Bushell et al., 2019; Stansfeld et al., 2015; Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Jiang et al., 2017; Khelashvili et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2022; Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021; Le et al., 2019b; Khelashvili et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data, comparison with atomistic simulations, and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through the scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore was observed, in line with the known ion-conducting capacity of these proteins.
claims.source: We also observed spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through the scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore (Appendix 1—figure 2B; number of permeation events in Source data 1), in line with the known ion-conducting capacity of these proteins (Yang et al., 2012; Martins et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2010; Malvezzi et al., 2013; Bushell et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; Scudieri et al., 2015; Falzone et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2022; Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data, comparison with experimental findings, and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Of the fungal structures, only the scrambling-competent open states sampled multiple ion permeation events with Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) showing highest conductance.
claims.source: Of the fungal structures, only the scrambling-competent open states sampled multiple ion permeation events with Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) showing highest conductance followed by Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), which was 3 times lower, and then Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), which was another three times lower again.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ion permeation from simulation data.

claims.claim: Cation-to-anion selectivity ratios of 5.1, 3.2, and 6 were measured for Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS), Ca2+-free nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), and Ca2+-bound afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), respectively.
claims.source: We also measured cation-to-anion selectivity ratios of 5.1, 3.2, and 6 for each simulation, respectively, computed from the ratio of total counts (PNa/PCl).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ion permeation from simulation data.

claims.claim: The simulations are consistent with experiments showing that both fungal scramblases transport anions and cations, and both are weakly cation selective.
claims.source: Our simulations are consistent with experiments showing that both fungal scramblases transport anions and cations (Lee et al., 2016), and both are weakly cation selective (PK/PCl = 1.5 for afTMEM16 based on experiment [Malvezzi et al., 2013] and PNa/PCl = 8.7 for nhTMEM16 based on AAMD [Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021]).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental and computational data from cited studies.

claims.claim: CGMD simulations sample ion conduction through open Ca2+-bound TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J, PNa/PCl = 1.3), which had the most ion permeation events.
claims.source: Our CGMD simulations also sample ion conduction through open Ca2+-bound TMEM16F F518H (PDB ID 8B8J, PNa/PCl = 1.3), which had the most ion permeation events (Hunter, 2007) across the family, simulated open TMEM16F (6QP6*, PNa/PCl = 0.33), and open TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9, PNa/PCl = 1.8).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ion permeation from simulation data.

claims.claim: The TMEM16K simulation result qualitatively agrees with experiment showing a slight cation preference.
claims.source: This latter result on TMEM16K qualitatively agrees with experiment showing a slight cation preference (Bushell et al., 2019), while experimental results for TMEM16F are more complex as its ion selectivity depends on membrane potential and divalent/monovalent cation concentrations (Nguyen et al., 2021; Stabilini et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from cited studies.

claims.claim: The simulation of the TMEM16F F518H mutant in 150 mM NaCl is most close to whole cell recordings performed in intracellular 150 mM NaCl and 15 μM Ca2+ where PNa/PCl = 1.0 ± 0.1, which is very similar to the simulated value of 1.3.
claims.source: Our simulation of the TMEM16F F518H mutant in 150 mM NaCl is most close to whole cell recordings performed in intracellular 150 mM NaCl and 15 μM Ca2+ where PNa/PCl = 1.0 ± 0.1 (Ye et al., 2019), which is very similar to our simulated value of 1.3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claims.claim: TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) had four Cl− and no Na+ permeation events, consistent with its experimentally measured anion selectivity (PNa/PCl = 0.1).
claims.source: Finally, TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) had four Cl− and no Na+ permeation events, consistent with its experimentally measured anion selectivity (PNa/PCl = 0.1; Peters et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claims.claim: No Cl− permeation was observed in any of the other computationally predicted TMEM16A structures (5OYB*, 7ZK3*8, and 7ZK3*10), while AAMD simulations of these structures all reported Cl− conduction.
claims.source: Interestingly, we did not observe Cl− permeation in any of the other computationally predicted TMEM16A structures (5OYB*, 7ZK3*8, and 7ZK3*10), while AAMD simulations of these structures all reported Cl− conduction (Jia and Chen, 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with other computational data from a cited study.

claims.claim: A minority of observed scrambling events (8%) occurred outside of the hydrophilic groove between TM4 and TM6.
claims.source: A minority of our observed scrambling events (8%) occurred outside of the hydrophilic groove between TM4 and TM6.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: Most out-of-the-groove scrambling events happened at the dimer interface with lipids inserting their headgroups into the cavity outlined by TM3 and TM10.
claims.source: Surprisingly, most of these events happened at the dimer interface with lipids inserting their headgroups into the cavity outlined by TM3 and TM10 (Figure 4A, B; Figure 2—figure supplements 2–5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: Out-of-the-groove scrambling at the dimer interface was only observed in simulations of the mammalian homologs.
claims.source: We only observed scrambling at this location in simulations of the mammalian homologs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claims.claim: In atomistic simulations of a closed Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (PDB ID 6QP6), a similar flipping event for a POPC lipid into the dimer interface was observed.
claims.source: In atomistic simulations of a closed Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (PDB ID 6QP6), we observed a similar flipping event for a POPC lipid into the dimer interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from atomistic simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The dimer interface is largely hydrophobic, but there are a few polar and charged residues in the cavity near the membrane core, and water is present in the lower half of the cavity.
claims.source: Although the dimer interface is largely hydrophobic, there are a few polar and charged residues in the cavity near the membrane core, and water is present in the lower half of the cavity (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The headgroup of the lipid in the atomistic simulation of TMEM16F interacts with a glutamate (E843) and lysine (K850) on TM10 near the membrane midplane.
claims.source: In fact, the headgroup of the lipid in our atomistic simulation of TMEM16F interacts with a glutamate (E843) and lysine (K850) on TM10 near the membrane midplane (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from atomistic simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Lipids that scramble at the dimer interface interact with the protein up to 10-fold longer on average than those in the canonical groove.
claims.source: Lipids that scramble at the dimer interface interact with the protein up to 10-fold longer on average than those in the canonical groove (Figure 4C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: The most prolonged interactions occur at sites containing aromatic residues into which the lipid tails intercalate.
claims.source: The most prolonged interactions occur at sites containing aromatic residues into which the lipid tails intercalate (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: One scrambling event occurred across a closed TM4/TM6 groove of Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (PDB ID 6P47), which is the only event that fits the postulated out-of-the-groove definition where scrambling is expected to take place near TM4/TM6 but without inserting into the groove.
claims.source: There were five more out-of-the-groove events, including one that occurred across a closed TM4/TM6 groove of Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (PDB ID 6P47). From all our observed scrambling events, this is the only one that fits the postulated out-of-the-groove definition where scrambling is expected to take place near TM4/TM6 but without inserting into the groove (Feng et al., 2024b; Appendix 1—figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Two scrambling events occurred concurrently along TM6 and TM8 near the hydrophilic groove of a Ca2+-bound closed TMEM16F (PDB ID 8TAG).
claims.source: Two events occurred concurrently along TM6 and TM8 again near the hydrophilic groove of a Ca2+-bound closed TMEM16F (PDB ID 8TAG; Appendix 1—figure 6A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Two scrambling events occurred along TM3 and TM4, one near the canonical TM4/TM6 groove of an open nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) and the other adjacent to the pore of an ion-conductive TMEM16A (7ZK3*8).
claims.source: Lastly, two events occurred along TM3 and TM4, one near the canonical TM4/TM6 groove of an open nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) and the other adjacent to the pore of an ion-conductive TMEM16A (7ZK3*8; Appendix 1—figure 6C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: In each of the five out-of-the-groove events, the scrambling lipid traverses with two to four water molecules around its headgroup.
claims.source: In each of these five out-of-the-groove events, the scrambling lipid traverses with two to four water molecules around its headgroup.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claims.claim: Previous all-atom simulations of TMEM16 have captured partial translocations or at most a handful of complete scrambling events due to the challenges inherent in simulating molecular events on the low microseconds time scale.
claims.source: Previous all-atom simulations of TMEM16 have captured partial translocations or – at most – a handful of complete scrambling events (e.g., Bethel and Grabe, 2016; Lee et al., 2018; Khelashvili et al., 2022) due to the challenges inherent in simulating molecular events on the low microseconds time scale.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on review of previous computational studies and identifies a limitation.

claims.claim: The small number of AAMD-derived scrambling events cannot provide rigorous statistics on scrambling rates, nor can they be leveraged to perform a large high-throughput comparison between the various family members.
claims.source: Although this small number of AAMD-derived scrambling events yielded key insights into specific protein–lipid interactions and scrambling pathways, they cannot provide rigorous statistics on scrambling rates, nor can they be leveraged to perform a large high-throughput comparison between the various family members.
claims.evidence: This claim is an assessment of the limitations of previous AAMD studies.

claims.claim: The study used CGMD to systematically quantify lipid scrambling by five TMEM16 family members and relate their scrambling competence to their structural characteristics and ability to distort the membrane.
claims.source: To circumvent sampling issues, we used CGMD to systematically quantify lipid scrambling by five TMEM16 family members and relate their scrambling competence to their structural characteristics and ability to distort the membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim describes the approach and goals of the study.

claims.claim: The simulations correctly differentiate between open and closed conformations across the five family members, consistent with a recent study showing good qualitative agreement between in vitro and in silico lipid scrambling using the same Martini 3 force field.
claims.source: Our simulations correctly differentiate between open and closed conformations across the five family members, consistent with a recent study that showed good qualitative agreement between in vitro and in silico lipid scrambling using the same Martini 3 force field on a diverse set of proteins, including some TMEM16s (Tsuji et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data and a cited validation study.

claims.claim: The simulation results are in accord with the general finding that TMEM16s show very little to no ion selectivity, although permeability ratios vary depending on ion concentrations and lipid environments.
claims.source: In addition to lipid scrambling ability, our results are in accord with the general finding that TMEM16s show very little to no ion selectivity, although permeability ratios vary depending on ion concentrations and lipid environments (Kostritskii and Machtens, 2021; Nguyen et al., 2021; Stabilini et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental findings from cited studies.

claims.claim: The study is in a unique position to directly compare a host of biophysical properties between different TMEM16 family members and their structures because the simulation conditions and system setups were identical in all simulations.
claims.source: Because the simulation conditions and system setups were identical in all our simulations, we are in a unique position to directly compare a host of biophysical properties between different TMEM16 family members and their structures to answer ongoing questions in the field.
claims.evidence: This claim highlights a methodological strength of the study.

claims.claim: Even non-scrambling, closed-groove structures elicit large membrane distortions.
claims.source: We (Bethel and Grabe, 2016) and others Bushell et al., 2019; Khelashvili et al., 2019; Falzone et al., 2022; Arndt et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2019 have hypothesized that thinning lowers the physical and energetic barrier for lipid scrambling, but what is surprising is that even non-scrambling, closed-groove structures elicit such large membrane distortions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and comparison with previous hypotheses.

claims.claim: Several of the closed-groove TMEM16F structures and the ion channel TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) compress the membrane 13–14 Å, yet these conformations do not induce scrambling.
claims.source: For instance, several of the closed-groove TMEM16F structures and the ion channel TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) compress the membrane 13–14 Å. Despite this large deformation, these conformations do not induce scrambling.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: Structures with dilated grooves exhibit robust scrambling and thin the membrane another 3–4 Å, resulting in the most distorted bilayers.
claims.source: On the other hand, structures with dilated grooves exhibit robust scrambling and thin the membrane another 3–4 Å, resulting in the most distorted bilayers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: Because extreme membrane thinning is coupled to lipid entry into the upper and lower vestibules upon groove opening, it is difficult to determine how much the membrane thinning alone contributes to the resulting scramblase activity.
claims.source: However, because this extreme membrane thinning is coupled to lipid entry into the upper and lower vestibules upon groove opening, it is difficult to determine how much the membrane thinning alone contributes to the resulting scramblase activity.
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the simulation data.

claims.claim: Groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling, and the importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
claims.evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: The importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling, and the importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges an open question that remains to be addressed.

claims.claim: The open-groove nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) is the fastest scrambler, with a rate twice as high as the other homologs.
claims.source: Of the scrambling-competent TMEM16 structures, the open-groove nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) is the fastest scrambler, with a rate twice as high as the other homologs (Figures 2A and 3A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in figures.

claims.claim: On average, the groove width and membrane thinning of nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 4WIS) are similar (within 1–2 Å) to the other robust scramblers nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), and TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9).
claims.source: Yet on average, its groove width and membrane thinning are similar (within 1–2 Å) to the other robust scramblers nhTMEM16 (PDB ID 6QM6), afTMEM16 (PDB ID 7RXG), and TMEM16K (PDB ID 5OC9) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: There are other features that impact scrambling rates, for example, the shape of the membrane distortion, groove dynamics, and residues lining the groove.
claims.source: This suggests that there are other features that impact the rates, for example, the shape of the membrane distortion, groove dynamics, and residues lining the groove.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the simulation data.

claims.claim: Mixed membranes and membranes of shorter or longer chain length would be expected to alter lipid scrambling rates.
claims.source: Another feature we have not explored is mixed membranes and membranes of shorter or longer chain length, which we expect would alter lipid scrambling rates.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about factors not explored in the study.

claims.claim: TMEM16K resides in the ER membrane which is thinner than the plasma membrane.
claims.source: For example, TMEM16K resides in the ER membrane which is thinner than the plasma membrane (Bushell et al., 2019; Petkovic et al., 2019; Bruininks et al., 2019), and TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes (Bushell et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and computational studies.

claims.claim: TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes.
claims.source: For example, TMEM16K resides in the ER membrane which is thinner than the plasma membrane (Bushell et al., 2019; Petkovic et al., 2019; Bruininks et al., 2019), and TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes (Bushell et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a computational study.

claims.claim: Experimental scrambling assays performed by different groups have reported basal level scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+ for fungal and mammalian dual-function scramblases.
claims.source: Experimental scrambling assays performed by different groups have reported basal level scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+ for fungal and mammalian dual-function scramblases (Malvezzi et al., 2013; Bushell et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2016; Brunner et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018; Malvezzi et al., 2018; Watanabe et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: It is unknown where closed-groove scrambling takes place on the protein.
claims.source: It is unknown where closed-groove scrambling takes place on the protein (Feng et al., 2024a) and simulations have never reported such events despite Li and co-workers reporting scrambling events for simulations initiated from closed TMEM16A, TMEM16K, and TMEM16F (Tsuji et al., 2019), which may have also been sampled in these trajectories.
claims.evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge and references a citation.

claims.claim: In aggregate, 60 scrambling events were observed that do not follow the credit card model and occur 'out-of-the-groove'.
claims.source: In aggregate, we observed 60 scrambling events that do not follow the credit card model and occur 'out-of-the-groove' (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is presented in a table.

claims.claim: Nearly all out-of-the-groove events (56/60) happen at the dimer interface between TM3 and TM10 of the opposite subunit.
claims.source: Nearly all these events (56/60) happen at the dimer interface between TM3 and TM10 of the opposite subunit, hereon referred to as the dimer cleft.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data.

claims.claim: No scrambling at the dimer cleft was observed for any of the fungal structures.
claims.source: Curiously, we do not observe scrambling at this location for any of the fungal structures.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claims.claim: Mammalian TMEM16s have a ~4–5 Å wider gap on average at the lower leaflet dimer cleft entrance than the open fungal TMEM16s.
claims.source: Although mammalian TMEM16s have a ~4–5 Å wider gap on average at the lower leaflet dimer cleft entrance than the open fungal TMEM16s, we do not always observe scrambling at such distances and sometimes do not observe any scrambling when the cleft is at its widest (Appendix 1—figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Lipids from both leaflets intercalate between TM3 and TM10 for all structures, which is consistent with lipid densities in cryo-EM nanodiscs images of fungal TMEM16s and TMEM16F.
claims.source: For all structures, we see lipids from both leaflets intercalate between TM3 and TM10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), which is consistent with lipid densities in cryo-EM nanodiscs images of fungal TMEM16s (Falzone et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024a) and TMEM16F (Feng et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and comparison with experimental cryo-EM data.

claims.claim: The dimer interface may be a source for Ca2+-independent scrambling.
claims.source: Based on our simulations, this interface may be a source for Ca2+-independent scrambling.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the simulation data, indicated by 'may be'.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether the out-of-the-groove events observed reflect the same closed-groove scrambling activity seen in experimental assays.
claims.source: It is unclear whether the out-of-the-groove events we have observed reflect the same closed-groove scrambling activity seen in experimental assays (Lee et al., 2018; Malvezzi et al., 2018; Falzone et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2024a).
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges uncertainty in interpreting the simulation results and references experimental studies.

claims.claim: It is possible that slow or rare out-of-the-groove events were missed due to limited sampling.
claims.source: Also, it is possible that we have missed slow or rare out-of-the-groove events due to limited sampling.
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges a potential limitation of the simulation study.

claims.claim: Feng et al. reported a 7- to 18-fold increase in scrambling rate by nhTMEM16 in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions.
claims.source: Feng et al. reported a 7- to 18-fold increase in scrambling rate by nhTMEM16 in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions (Feng et al., 2024a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: Based on the open-groove count of 220 for nhTMEM16, 12–30 events would be expected for the closed-groove states, but no events were observed.
claims.source: Based on our open-groove count of 220, we would expect 12–30 events for the closed-groove states, but we observed no events.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on calculation from simulation data and comparison with experimental ratios.

claims.claim: Watanabe et al. reported a six- to seven-fold increase in scrambling rate by TMEM16F in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions.
claims.source: However, Watanabe et al. reported a six- to seven-fold increase in scrambling rate by TMEM16F in the presence of Ca2+ compared to Ca2+-free conditions (Watanabe et al., 2018), which is consistent with the seven- to nine-fold increase revealed in our simulations between closed Ca2+-free TMEM16F structures (PBD IDs 6P47 and 6QPB) and the WT open Ca2+-bound TMEM16F (6QP6*).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claims.claim: Out-of-the-groove scrambling may be highly dependent on the membrane composition, and the scrambling ratios observed in DOPC may be different from the experimental rates determined in different lipids.
claims.source: It is possible that out-of-the-groove scrambling is highly dependent on the membrane composition, as discussed earlier, and the scrambling ratios we observe in DOPC may be different from the experimental rates determined in different lipids.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about factors that may affect the results.

claims.claim: The simulations observe much higher scrambling rates through the open grooves and much smaller flipping rates elsewhere on the protein or with closed-groove structures, suggesting that the simulations may be revealing aspects of Ca2+-independent scrambling in mammalian family members.
claims.source: That said, we are encouraged by the high-level correspondence in TMEM16F – we observe much higher scrambling rates through the open grooves and much smaller flipping rates elsewhere on the protein or with closed-groove structures, suggesting that our simulations may be revealing aspects of Ca2+-independent scrambling in mammalian family members.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the simulation results, indicated by 'suggesting' and 'may be revealing'.

claims.claim: The simulations correctly distinguish scrambling-competent structures from non-competent scramblers, but direct comparison of simulation rates with experimental values should be interpreted qualitatively.
claims.source: With regard to predicting absolute rates, our simulations correctly distinguish scrambling-competent structures from non-competent scramblers, but direct comparison of our rates with experimental values (that tend to be 2–3 orders of magnitude slower) should be interpreted qualitatively.
claims.evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation in quantitative comparison between simulation and experiment.

claims.claim: Single-molecule analysis yielded a scrambling rate of 0.04 events per μs for TMEM16F, whereas the simulations find 3 and 11.3 events per μs for scrambling-competent TMEM16F structures 6QP6* and PDB ID 8B8J, respectively.
claims.source: For example, single-molecule analysis yielded a scrambling rate of 0.04 events per μs for TMEM16F (Watanabe et al., 2018), whereas we find 3 and 11.3 events per μs for our scrambling-competent TMEM16F structures 6QP6* and PDB ID 8B8J, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claims.claim: Malvezzi et al. estimated a scrambling rate of 0.02 events per μs for afTMEM16 using a liposome-based assay, while the simulations find 10.7 events per μs.
claims.source: Malvezzi et al. estimated a similar scrambling rate of 0.02 events per μs for afTMEM16 using a liposome-based assay, while we find 10.7 events per μs (Malvezzi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data from a cited study.

claims.claim: The Martini model increases diffusion dynamics by a factor ~4 due to the lower friction between CG beads and reduced configurational entropy compared to more chemically detailed representations.
claims.source: First, it is well established that the Martini model increases diffusion dynamics by a factor ~4 due to the lower friction between CG beads and reduced configurational entropy compared to more chemically detailed representations (Bruininks et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on the Martini force field.

claims.claim: The energy barrier for a PC headgroup to traverse the DOPC bilayer in the absence of protein is reduced in Martini 3 compared to Martini 2 and AAMD.
claims.source: Second, the energy barrier for a PC headgroup to traverse the DOPC bilayer in the absence of protein is reduced in Martini 3 compared to Martini 2 and AAMD (Bartoš et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing force fields.

claims.claim: It is not trivial to predict how the reduction in energy barrier affects protein-mediated lipid scrambling, but it is likely to increase observed flipping rates compared to the more realistic AAMD.
claims.source: It is not trivial to predict how this reduction affects protein-mediated lipid scrambling, but it is likely to increase observed flipping rates compared to the more realistic AAMD.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about the effect of force field differences on simulation results.

claims.claim: The Martini 3 elastic network used to restrain the protein backbone allows a small degree of flexibility during simulations, which may increase scrambling.
claims.source: Third, as shown in Figure 3B, the Martini 3 elastic network used to restrain the protein backbone in our simulations allows a small degree of flexibility during simulations, which may increase scrambling.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about the effect of the elastic network on simulation results and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The groove of the open nhTMEM16 structure 4WIS enlarges by ~3 Å during Martini 3 simulations compared to the starting experimental structure and Martini 2 simulations, and this dilation correlates with greater scrambling.
claims.source: For instance, the groove of the open nhTMEM16 structure 4WIS enlarges by ~3 Å during our Martini 3 simulations compared to the starting experimental structure and our Martini 2 simulations, and this dilation correlates with greater scrambling (Appendix 1—figure 8A, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: CHARMM36 AAMD trajectories of nhTMEM16 show some degree of dilation, but they generally stay closer to the experimental structure than Martini 3 simulations.
claims.source: We also analyzed previously published CHARMM36 AAMD trajectories starting from the same structure (Bethel and Grabe, 2016) and observed that while these simulations do show some degree of dilation, as we observe with Martini 3, they generally stay closer to the experimental structure (Appendix 1—figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of previously published AAMD data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: Similar subtle movements in the TM4 helix were observed for open Ca2+-bound structures of afTMEM16, TMEM16K, TMEM16F, and TMEM16A that appear to enlarge the TM4/TM6 outer vestibule.
claims.source: In addition to the open nhTMEM16 structure, we observed similar subtle movements in the TM4 helix for open Ca2+-bound structures of afTMEM16, TMEM16K, TMEM16F, and TMEM16A that appear to enlarge the TM4/TM6 outer vestibule (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: AAMD simulations have reported that spontaneous dilation of the groove/pore can confer either scramblase activity for WT and mutant TMEM16F or ion channel activity for TMEM16A structures.
claims.source: Others have reported that AAMD simulations sample spontaneous dilation of the groove/pore to confer either scramblase activity for WT (Le et al., 2019b; Khelashvili et al., 2022) and mutant (Jia et al., 2022) TMEM16F or ion channel activity for TMEM16A structures (Le et al., 2019a; Yu et al., 2019; Tembo et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to computational studies.

claims.claim: Movements away from the experimentally solved structures may be due to the inaccuracy of atomistic and CG force fields or differences in the model and experimental membrane/detergent environments.
claims.source: These movements away from the experimentally solved structures may be due to the inaccuracy of our atomistic and CG force fields or differences in the model and experimental membrane/detergent environments, but more work is needed to assess whether these dilations reflect physiologically relevant conformational states.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about the causes of observed structural changes in simulations.

claims.claim: CG simulations of closed-groove structures lack dilations because the backbones of TM4 and TM6 are in close enough proximity (<10 Å) to be connected by the elastic network that the Martini model requires to maintain proper secondary and tertiary structure.
claims.source: CG simulations of closed-groove structures lack such dilations, because the backbones of TM4 and TM6 are in close enough proximity (<10 Å) to be connected by the elastic network that the Martini model requires to maintain proper secondary and tertiary structure (e.g., PDB ID 6QM4, see Appendix 1—figure 8C, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is an explanation for the observed behavior in simulations and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The recent GōMartini 3 model replaces the harmonic bonds of the elastic network with Lennard–Jones potentials that vanish as residues separate, potentially making this an excellent model for sampling groove opening and closing.
claims.source: The recent GōMartini 3 model replaces the harmonic bonds of the elastic network with Lennard–Jones potentials that vanish as residues separate, potentially making this an excellent model for sampling groove opening and closing (Souza et al., 2024; Appendix 1—figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about the potential of a new force field model and is supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: The low number of recorded scrambling events for TMEM16A (11 for the highest and 1 for the lowest) may be consistent with the lack of experimentally measured scramblase activity.
claims.source: Finally, we end by discussing the observed in- and out-of-the-groove scrambling for the putative ion-conducting states of TMEM16A. The low number of recorded events (11 for the highest and 1 for the lowest) may be consistent with the lack of experimentally measured scramblase activity (Han et al., 2019; Gyobu et al., 2017), for the reasons discussed in the last paragraph.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of simulation results in light of experimental data.

claims.claim: An energy barrier for lipid movement through the TMEM16A groove was computed to be 5.5-fold higher than the scramblase barriers.
claims.source: Consistent with our low computational rate, we also computed an energy barrier for lipid movement through the TMEM16A groove 5.5-fold higher than the scramblase barriers (Appendix 1—figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by free energy calculations from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: In simulations of three predicted ion-conductive states of TMEM16A (7ZK3*6,8,10) lipid headgroups insert into the lower and upper vestibule of the pore.
claims.source: In simulations of our three predicted ion-conductive states of TMEM16A (7ZK3*6,8,10) lipid headgroups insert into the lower and upper vestibule of the pore.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claims.claim: Compared to the inhibitor-bound structure (PDB ID 7ZK3), the outer vestibule of the conductive states of TMEM16A is notably more dilated.
claims.source: Compared to the inhibitor-bound structure (PDB ID 7ZK3), the outer vestibule of these conductive states is notably more dilated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison from simulation data.

claims.claim: Four Cl− permeation events by TMEM16A (7ZK3*8) were observed through the partially lipid-lined groove.
claims.source: We observe four Cl− permeation events by 7ZK3*8 through the partially lipid-lined groove.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data.

claims.claim: The simulation of the predicted TMEM16A conductive state from Jia and Chen at times featured a fully lipid-lined groove, similar to the proteolipidic pore found in dual-function members.
claims.source: Surprisingly, our simulation of the predicted TMEM16A conductive state from Jia and Chen did at times feature a fully lipid-lined groove, similar to the proteolipidic pore found in dual-function members (Jia and Chen, 2021; Figure 1D, Figure 3—video 1); however, we did not observe any ion permeation events from this configuration, which may be a consequence of the configuration not being physiologically relevant, the Martini 3 force field not being ideal for Cl−/lipid/protein interactions, or something else.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure and video.

claims.claim: No ion permeation events were observed from the fully lipid-lined groove configuration of TMEM16A, which may be a consequence of the configuration not being physiologically relevant, the Martini 3 force field not being ideal for Cl−/lipid/protein interactions, or something else.
claims.source: Surprisingly, our simulation of the predicted TMEM16A conductive state from Jia and Chen did at times feature a fully lipid-lined groove, similar to the proteolipidic pore found in dual-function members (Jia and Chen, 2021; Figure 1D, Figure 3—video 1); however, we did not observe any ion permeation events from this configuration, which may be a consequence of the configuration not being physiologically relevant, the Martini 3 force field not being ideal for Cl−/lipid/protein interactions, or something else.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation about possible explanations for the simulation results.

claims.claim: It is intriguing that while TMEM16A has lost experimentally discernible scrambling activity, it still deforms and thins the membrane.
claims.source: It is intriguing that while TMEM16A has lost experimentally discernible scrambling activity, it still deforms and thins the membrane (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is an observation from simulation data and is illustrated in a figure.

claims.claim: TMEM16A may retain thinning capabilities to facilitate partial lipid insertion to promote Cl- permeation.
claims.source: Coupled with our observation that groove widening allows lipids to enter, we wonder if it retains thinning capabilities to facilitate partial lipid insertion to promote Cl- permeation. This hypothesis has been stated before (Whitlock and Hartzell, 2016), and structural evidence for this proteolipidic ion channel pore has recently been reported for the OSCA1.2 mechanosensitive ion channel, which adopts the TMEM16 fold, yet it does not scramble lipids (Lowry et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation supported by citations to previous hypotheses and recent structural evidence.

results.result: The study performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations of 27 structures from five different TMEM16 family members and captured over 700 scrambling events in aggregate. This comprehensive computational approach enabled systematic quantification of lipid scrambling across fungal and mammalian TMEM16s.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C55, and C153 describe the core methodology and scope of the study. The quantitative results (27 structures, >700 events) are directly stated and form the foundation for all subsequent analyses. The methodology is clearly described and appropriate for the research questions.

results.result: CGMD using the Martini 3 force field was validated as an appropriate method for studying TMEM16 scrambling, as it correctly differentiates between open and closed conformations and shows good qualitative agreement with experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C57, and C154 establish the validity of the computational approach. The validation is supported by comparison with experimental data and previous computational studies. The choice of CGMD is justified by its ability to reach longer timescales while maintaining chemical detail.

results.result: The CGMD simulations successfully reproduce experimentally determined membrane deformations seen in cryo-EM nanodiscs across both fungal and mammalian TMEM16s, including sinusoidal curves, differential membrane shapes between fungal and mammalian members, and lipid density patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C66, C67, C68, C69, C70, C71, and C75 demonstrate that the simulations accurately reproduce experimental observations. The qualitative agreement with cryo-EM data, AAMD simulations, and continuum models validates the simulation approach and provides confidence in the results.

results.result: All TMEM16 structures thin the membrane by at least 7 Å (to 23 Å or less), regardless of scrambling activity. Even non-scrambling, closed-groove structures elicit large membrane distortions (13-14 Å compression), while structures with dilated grooves thin the membrane an additional 3-4 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C100, C157, C158, and C159 establish that membrane thinning is a universal feature of TMEM16 proteins but is not sufficient for scrambling. The quantitative measurements are consistent across multiple structures and provide clear evidence that membrane thinning alone does not determine scrambling activity.

results.result: The majority of scrambling (>90%) occurs at the groove only when TM4 and TM6 have sufficiently separated (>6 Å) and the membrane is thinned to at least 14 Å. Groove dilation is the ultimate trigger for rapid lipid scrambling.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C99, C101, C102, C103, C108, and C161 establish the primary mechanism of scrambling. The quantitative thresholds (>6 Å TM4-TM6 distance, <14 Å membrane thickness) are empirically determined from the simulation data and consistently predict scrambling competence across all structures.

results.result: Only open scramblase structures have grooves fully lined by lipids (typically 2-3 lipids at any given time), and these structures promote scrambling with lipids experiencing a less than 1 kT free energy barrier. All grooves are filled with water, but only open grooves allow lipid headgroups to span the bilayer.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, C74, C76, C77, and C78 describe the structural requirements for scrambling. The lipid density analysis, free energy calculations, and water content measurements provide converging evidence for the credit card model of scrambling through an open, hydrated groove.

results.result: Scrambling rates vary across TMEM16 family members and conformational states. Open Ca2+-bound nhTMEM16 (4WIS) is the fastest scrambler (24.4±5.2 events/μs), while closed-groove structures show negligible scrambling. TMEM16K shows asymmetric scrambling between monomers, and wild-type TMEM16F structures show little to no scrambling, except for the F518H mutant (11.3±1.6 events/μs) and a simulated open structure (3.0±1.6 events/μs).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C89, C91, C94, C95, and C97 provide quantitative scrambling rates across multiple structures. The rates are consistently measured using the same methodology, allowing direct comparison. The results correctly distinguish scrambling-competent from non-competent structures and are consistent with experimental observations.

results.result: One simulation of TMEM16A initiated from a predicted ion-conductive state scrambled lipids through a lipid-lined groove at a very low rate (only two events), suggesting that ion channel-only members may have residual non-detectable scramblase activity. The predicted ion-conductive state samples an average TM4-TM6 distance just below the 6 Å threshold for scrambling.
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C62, C98, C114, C115, and C116 describe rare scrambling events in TMEM16A. While the observations are reported, the interpretation that this represents 'residual scramblase activity' is speculative (indicated by 'suggesting' and 'may have'). The low event count (2 events) makes it difficult to distinguish from statistical noise or force field artifacts.

results.result: While scrambling rates are generally higher with thinner membranes and wider grooves, lipids flowing into the upper and lower vestibules of dilated grooves heavily contribute to the observed extreme membrane thinning (<14 Å). The extremely thin membranes are likely correlated with groove opening rather than being an independent contributing factor to lipid scrambling. The importance of membrane thinning to modulating scrambling rates has yet to be determined.
results.evaluation: Claims C105, C106, C107, C160, and C162 address the relationship between membrane thinning and scrambling. The analysis correctly identifies that extreme thinning is coupled to lipid entry into the groove, making it difficult to separate the effects. The conclusion that groove dilation is the primary determinant is well-supported, though the authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about the independent contribution of thinning.

results.result: Hydrophobic residues at the midpoint of the TMEM16F and TMEM16K pathways dynamically swing open to sporadically allow lipids through. Scrambling occurs more frequently when the groove is open, with the subunit spending more time in an open-groove configuration showing higher scrambling activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C109, C110, C111, C112, and C113 describe the dynamic nature of groove opening in TMEM16F and TMEM16K. The observations are supported by time-resolved analysis of groove distances and scrambling events, showing clear correlation between groove opening and scrambling frequency.

results.result: Despite individual differences in groove dynamics, scrambling occurs in an identical manner across the TMEM16 family. Scrambling lipids move through the TM4/TM6 groove quickly (dwell times <20 ns) with a barrierless free energy profile (<1 kT). Scrambling events enter and leave the groove at random locations and are Poisson distributed, indicating lipids do not scramble in a regular or kinetically coordinated fashion.
results.evaluation: Claims C117, C118, C119, C120, C121, C124, and C125 characterize the mechanism and kinetics of scrambling. The free energy calculations, dwell time measurements, and statistical analysis of event distributions provide strong evidence for a common scrambling mechanism across the family with stochastic lipid entry and exit.

results.result: Four residues (E313, R432, K353, and E352) at the intracellular and extracellular entrances of the nhTMEM16 groove were previously hypothesized to help organize or stabilize scrambling lipids. However, CGMD shows that although these residues have elevated contact frequencies, more than half of the contacts are made with bulk lipids that never scramble.
results.evaluation: Claims C122 and C123 re-evaluate a previous hypothesis using the new CGMD data. The quantitative analysis of lipid contacts demonstrates that the previously identified residues are not specifically involved in organizing scrambling lipids, as they interact predominantly with non-scrambling lipids. This is a well-supported revision of a prior hypothesis.

results.result: Water permeation through closed scramblase structures is low (<30 events/μs), while dilated TM4/TM6 grooves support 300-550 permeation events/μs. Even when the groove is inaccessible to lipids in closed states, it remains hydrated with waters shielded from the hydrophobic core. In open grooves, water is exposed to the membrane core and lipid headgroups occupy the fully hydrated groove to bridge the leaflets.
results.evaluation: Claims C126, C127, C128, and C129 characterize water content in the groove. The quantitative measurements of water permeation events and qualitative observations of hydration patterns are consistent with the credit card model and provide additional support for the mechanism of scrambling through a hydrated groove.

results.result: Spontaneous permeation of Na+ and Cl− ions through scramblase TMEM16 grooves and TMEM16A pore was observed, consistent with the known ion-conducting capacity of these proteins. The simulations show weak cation selectivity for fungal scramblases and reproduce experimentally measured selectivity ratios for TMEM16F F518H and TMEM16A.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137 and C155 demonstrate that the simulations capture ion permeation in addition to lipid scrambling. The selectivity ratios are generally consistent with experimental measurements, though the authors appropriately note statistical limitations for structures with few events. The agreement with experiment validates the simulation approach.

results.result: No Cl− permeation was observed in computationally predicted TMEM16A structures (5OYB*, 7ZK3*8, and 7ZK3*10) in CGMD, while AAMD simulations of these structures all reported Cl− conduction.
results.evaluation: Claim C138 identifies a discrepancy between CGMD and AAMD results for TMEM16A ion conduction. This is a valid observation that highlights potential limitations of the CGMD approach for ion permeation, though the authors do not fully explore the reasons for this discrepancy.

results.result: 60 scrambling events (8% of total) occurred outside the canonical groove, with 56/60 (>90%) taking place at the dimer-dimer interface between TM3 and TM10 in mammalian TMEM16s. This dimer interface represents an alternative mechanism for lipid scrambling in the absence of an open groove. No scrambling at the dimer cleft was observed for fungal structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C11, C139, C140, C141, C171, C172, and C173 describe a novel finding of out-of-the-groove scrambling. The quantitative data clearly show that this occurs predominantly at the dimer interface in mammalian structures. While the functional significance is uncertain, the observation itself is well-documented.

results.result: In atomistic simulations of closed Ca2+-bound TMEM16F, a similar flipping event for a POPC lipid into the dimer interface was observed. The dimer interface is largely hydrophobic but contains polar and charged residues near the membrane core with water present in the lower half. Lipids that scramble at the dimer interface interact with the protein up to 10-fold longer than those in the canonical groove, with the most prolonged interactions occurring at sites containing aromatic residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C142, C143, C144, C145, C146, C174, and C175 provide structural and kinetic characterization of dimer interface scrambling. The atomistic simulation provides independent validation of the CGMD observation. The structural analysis and dwell time measurements are well-documented and support the existence of this alternative pathway.

results.result: Five additional out-of-the-groove scrambling events were observed at various locations: one across a closed TM4/TM6 groove (the only event fitting the postulated out-of-the-groove definition), two along TM6 and TM8, and two along TM3 and TM4. In each case, the scrambling lipid traverses with 2-4 water molecules around its headgroup.
results.evaluation: Claims C147, C148, C149, and C150 document rare scrambling events at locations other than the canonical groove or dimer interface. While the events are few, they are clearly documented and characterized. The presence of water molecules suggests these may represent genuine scrambling pathways, though their physiological relevance is uncertain.

results.result: The dimer interface may be a source for Ca2+-independent scrambling. It is unclear whether the out-of-the-groove events observed reflect the same closed-groove scrambling activity seen in experimental assays. Comparison with experimental Ca2+-dependent fold-changes shows mixed agreement: nhTMEM16 simulations predict 12-30 events for closed-groove states but observed none, while TMEM16F simulations show a 7- to 9-fold increase consistent with experimental 6- to 7-fold increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C176, C177, C178, C179, C180, C181, C182, and C183 attempt to relate the out-of-the-groove scrambling to experimental observations of Ca2+-independent activity. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty and potential limitations (sampling, membrane composition). The mixed agreement with experimental fold-changes suggests the simulations may capture some aspects of Ca2+-independent scrambling but not others.

results.result: The simulations correctly distinguish scrambling-competent structures from non-competent scramblers, but direct comparison of simulation rates with experimental values (which are 2-3 orders of magnitude slower) should be interpreted qualitatively. Three factors contribute to faster simulated rates: (1) Martini model increases diffusion dynamics by ~4-fold, (2) reduced energy barrier for lipid flip in Martini 3, and (3) elastic network allows groove dilation during simulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C193 provide a critical assessment of the quantitative accuracy of the simulations. The authors appropriately acknowledge that absolute rates are overestimated while qualitative predictions are reliable. The three explanations for faster rates are well-supported by citations and analysis of groove dilation. This honest assessment of limitations strengthens confidence in the qualitative conclusions.

results.result: AAMD simulations have reported spontaneous dilation of the groove/pore to confer scramblase or ion channel activity. Movements away from experimentally solved structures may be due to force field inaccuracy or differences in membrane/detergent environments. CG simulations of closed-groove structures lack dilations because TM4 and TM6 backbones are connected by the elastic network. The GōMartini 3 model may be better for sampling groove opening and closing.
results.evaluation: Claims C194, C195, C196, and C197 discuss the structural dynamics observed in simulations and their relationship to experimental structures. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about whether observed dilations reflect physiologically relevant states and suggest potential improvements (GōMartini 3). This is a balanced assessment of methodological limitations.

results.result: The low number of scrambling events for TMEM16A (11 for the highest, 1 for the lowest) may be consistent with lack of experimentally measured scramblase activity. An energy barrier for lipid movement through the TMEM16A groove was 5.5-fold higher than scramblase barriers. In simulations of predicted ion-conductive states, lipid headgroups insert into the pore vestibules, and the outer vestibule is notably more dilated than the inhibitor-bound structure. TMEM16A may retain thinning capabilities to facilitate partial lipid insertion to promote Cl- permeation.
results.evaluation: Claims C198-C206 discuss TMEM16A scrambling and ion conduction. The observations are documented, but the interpretations are speculative (indicated by 'may be'). The hypothesis that TMEM16A retains thinning to facilitate a proteolipidic ion channel is interesting but requires experimental validation. The discrepancy between CGMD and AAMD for ion conduction is noted but not fully resolved.

results.result: Most scrambling in the groove occurs when the membrane is thinned to at least 14 Å and the groove is open. The study observed 218 ion permeation events but only in well-hydrated systems with open grooves (98%) and a closed-groove TMEM16A structure (2%). The simulations reveal alternative scrambling pathways, which primarily occur at the dimer-dimer interface in mammalian structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C64, and C65 summarize key findings from the study. These are well-supported by the quantitative data presented throughout the manuscript and represent the main conclusions of the work.

results.result: Previous all-atom simulations captured at most a handful of complete scrambling events due to timescale limitations and cannot provide rigorous statistics on scrambling rates or enable large high-throughput comparisons. The current study is in a unique position to directly compare biophysical properties between different TMEM16 family members because simulation conditions and system setups were identical.
results.evaluation: Claims C151, C152, and C156 establish the motivation and advantage of the current study. The assessment of previous work is accurate, and the methodological strength of using identical conditions for all simulations is correctly identified as enabling direct comparisons.

results.result: The open-groove nhTMEM16 (4WIS) is the fastest scrambler with a rate twice as high as other homologs, yet its groove width and membrane thinning are similar (within 1-2 Å) to other robust scramblers. This suggests other features impact scrambling rates, such as membrane distortion shape, groove dynamics, and residues lining the groove. Mixed membranes and different chain lengths would be expected to alter scrambling rates, as TMEM16K scrambling rates increase 10-fold in thinner membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C163, C164, C165, C166, C167, and C168 identify factors beyond groove width and membrane thinning that influence scrambling rates. The observations are well-supported by the data, and the speculation about additional factors (C165, C166) is reasonable and appropriately qualified. The citation about TMEM16K in thinner membranes (C168) provides experimental support.

results.result: Experimental scrambling assays have reported basal level scramblase activity in the absence of Ca2+ for fungal and mammalian dual-function scramblases. It is unknown where closed-groove scrambling takes place on the protein, and simulations have never reported such events.
results.evaluation: Claims C169 and C170 establish the context for the out-of-the-groove scrambling observations. The citations support the existence of Ca2+-independent scrambling in experiments, and the statement that simulations have not captured this is accurate based on the literature review.

results.result: The study employed coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) simulations of 27 structures from five different TMEM16 family members, capturing over 700 scrambling events. CGMD was chosen as it enables reaching longer time scales while retaining sufficient chemical detail to reproduce experimentally verified protein-lipid interactions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers across all reviews acknowledge the comprehensive nature of the CGMD approach and the large number of scrambling events captured. Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'the study demonstrates an efficient use of CGMD simulations' and that the authors 'bypass some of the sampling limitations inherent in all-atom simulations.' The editor and reviewers recognize this as a strength of the study.

results.result: All TMEM16 structures thin the membrane to 23 Å or less (at least 7 Å thinner than bulk), regardless of scrambling activity. Even non-scrambling, closed-groove structures elicit large membrane distortions (13-14 Å compression), while structures with dilated grooves thin the membrane an additional 3-4 Å.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the membrane thinning observations.
